line: [Intro] Sit down and drink some champagne with me and let me rap
vault_lines: Sit down and drink some champagne with me and let me rap
meaning:
The intro for this song samples Irene Reid’s “Didn’t We,” a soft and empowering release of 1971. Irene was a jazz singer raised in Savannah, Georgia who gained notoriety by leading in musicals and touring with live orchestras. Today, she is remembered by the titles of “the Blue Diva” and “Queen of Soul” and was even inducted into Savannah’s hall of fame in 1994. Irene managed to captivate listeners and left an undeniable imprint on soul in the state of New York, where she passed away in 2008.



Reid on the vinyl for her 1968 record I’ve Been Here All the Time


The first notable use of this sample can be traced back to the intro of 2003’s “Came Back for You” by Lil' Kim. Kanye West—who produced the aforementioned track—also sampled “Didn’t We” on “Half Price” the same year. Unlike the previous songs, Keem only partially samples the track which smoothly transitions into the more upbeat instrumental.

In monotheistic belief systems, God is usually viewed as the supreme being, creator, and principal object of faith.

In polytheistic belief systems, a god is “a spirit or being believed to have created, or for controlling some part of the universe or life, for which such a deity is often worshipped”.

Belief in the existence of at least one god is called theism.

Conceptions of God vary considerably.

Many notable theologians and philosophers have developed arguments for and against the existence of God.

Atheism rejects the belief in any deity. Agnosticism is the belief that the existence of God is unknown or unknowable.

Some theists view knowledge concerning God as derived from faith. God is often conceived as the greatest entity in existence.

God is often believed to be the cause of all things and so is seen as the creator, sustainer, and ruler of the universe. God is often thought of as incorporeal and independent of the material creation, while pantheism holds that God is the universe itself.

God is sometimes seen as omnibenevolent, while deism holds that God is not involved with humanity apart from creation.

Some traditions attach spiritual significance to maintaining some form of relationship with God, often involving acts such as worship and prayer, and see God as the source of all moral obligation.

God is sometimes described without reference to gender, while others use terminology that is gender-specific.

God is referred to by different names depending on the language and cultural tradition, sometimes with different titles of God used in reference to God’s various attributes.

The repetition of “two hoes” is a common theme in Keem’s discography. Although the lyrics could have many interpretations, they could tie into his alter ego of “Two-phone Baby Keem,” a sly and cunning gangster version of himself often referenced in past songs. Keem keeps multiple burner phones because they’re inexpensive and easy to replace—in a similar fashion, he claims to be recognizable with two hoes because there are no strings attached compared to an otherwise committed relationship.

On “range brothers”—one of the 2021 collaborations with his cousin Kendrick Lamar—Keem opens the song by rapping:

Two hoes and I think I did too much
I got two phones and I don’t know who to trust

Likewise, on “durag activity,” (also released as a part of 2021’s The Melodic Blue) Keem says this on the track’s third verse:

Don’t be eyeballin' your sister, ho-ho, smokin' mystical

line: I had to go see the doc like Kool Moe Dee (Yeah) Never took much to convince Dre Never been swayed by color or skin shade
vault_lines: I had to go see the doc like Kool Moe Dee (Yeah)
meaning:
Eminem sheds light on his friendship and professional relationship with his mentor and long-time producer Dr. Dre. Dre discovered Eminem in the late ‘90s and would help his career take off, producing tracks on his albums beginning with 1999’s The Slim Shady LP.

Since the start of Eminem’s career, he has received criticism for taking advantage of a historically African-American art form and becoming extremely successful. However, Dre has never judged Em for his ethnicity.



Note the wordplay with “swayed” and “shades”. Eminem gives a shout-out to Sway Calloway, who hosts a show on Em’s hip-hop radio station Shade 45.

Going to “see the doctor” refers to getting help from Dr. Dre and this is not the first time this expression has been used, and is notably focused on in Dre’s 2011 track “I Need a Doctor,” which also features Eminem.

Additionally, Em gives a shoutout to 1980s rap pioneer Kool Moe Dee and his gonorrhoea-themed 1986 song “Go See the Doctor.” He also gave Dee a shoutout on his verse from another track on this record, “Yah Yah.”

line: And for any of those who may have come close to about dyin’ And can’t listen to “Arose” without cryin’

meaning:
Referring to Arose, the final track of Eminem’s 2017 album, Revival. The song is an emotional one, being about Eminem’s near-death in 2007 due to a pill overdose. He raps about his family, friends and career in his dying moments before the song switches to an alternate ending of the previous track, Castle, where he dumps his pills down the toilet, rather than taking them and overdosing.

He is also talking about how his music is said to have kept people alive in suicidal moments. He talks about this in “Sing for the Moment” with the lyrics:

Or for anyone who’s ever been through shit in they lives
So they sit and they cry at night, wishin' they’d die
‘Til they throw on a rap record and they sit and they vibe

He knows how powerful his music is and how many people he’s helped, and for that, he would go through all the pain in his life again instead of changing anything, he literally has no regrets.

vault_lines: But sometimes it's like droppin' an anvil on a house of cards
meaning:
Eminem uses three similes to show the extent he’s willing to go to obliterate his adversaries and overproportionalize their affronts. These lines may sound familiar to the faint ear, as Eminem made a similar comparison on September 2018’s “Killshot,” his response to Machine Gun Kelly’s diss “RAP DEVIL”:

But you’re a fuckin' mole hill
Now I'ma make a mountain out of you, woo!

The producer of “No Regrets,” D.A. Doman, also produced fellow Music To Be Murdered By track “Godzilla,” to which Eminem alludes in these lines.

line: For some adversaries, I carry big guns So some targets’ll get the kill shot (Yeah) Some, I just barely nicked ’em

meaning:
“Big guns” and “kill shot” refer to Eminem’s widely publicized conflict with Machine Gun Kelly, while “Nicked ‘em” is a word play on Nick Cannon’s name, whose diss tracks Eminem mostly ignored. “Carry” likely alludes to Cannon’s ex-wife, Mariah Carey.

Eminem began feuding with MGK after he called Em’s then 16-year-old daughter “hot as fuck” in 2012. Em discussed the incident and his distaste for MGK on his 2018 surprise album Kamikaze, particularly on “Not Alike”:

You already know who the fuck you are, Kelly
I don’t use sublims and sure as fuck don’t sneak-diss
But keep commenting on my daughter Hailie

MGK responded with “RAP DEVIL,” and Em ended the series of diss tracks with “Killshot.” MGK alluded to the song on July 2019’s “Floor 13”.

Shortly after concluding his conflict with MGK, Em got involved in a feud with Nick Cannon. Cannon wrote “The Invitation” as a diss track, which received very poor reviews, and he released “Used to Look Up To You” just days before Music to Be Murdered By came out.

Cannon spoke about Em’s three daughters on “The Invitation,” focusing on his adopted daughters, Whitney and Alaina:

Call Kim, somebody get Hailie
And that other kid you raisin', that ain’t even your baby (Daddy)

By saying, “You fuck with a rat, I don’t fuck with them,” Don could be indirectly addressing this situation, expressing disdain for those who associate with figures accused of disloyalty.

vault_lines: I wanna go to the moon, don't leave so soon (Don't leave so soon)
meaning:
The song’s chorus draws inspiration from Kid Cudi’s acclaimed Man on the Moon trilogy of albums:


The End of Day
The Legend of Mr. Rager
The Chosen

In 2009, when asked about the symbolic meaning of the moon in the trilogy’s context, Cudi said:

The moon is pretty much my place of peace, whether it’s a room or my mind. It’s really your own personal space. It could be interpreted any different way. I didn’t wanna have it so literal. I want kids to interpret it and find their own moon in their world.

Here, getting to the moon can mean many things, from attaining a goal that is almost unreachable, to, especially in the context of Donda, a more spiritual ascension, seen through the reverbed vocals and echoing voices, similar to that in a large chapel. Kanye’s answer to how he could get to the moon and “how could I get through,” might be through Jesus, following on the gospel message of the album.

Moreover, the moon is used not only as a metaphor for a peaceful place, but also for death. Throughout the chorus, Toliver sings “don’t leave so soon,” which is in reference to suicide. In this context, the moon represents death, as he urges the listener not to leave the earth by ending their life prematurely. Further, in every second line, he follows the line by saying “how can I get through,” which is a double entendre for:


How can he get to a peaceful place (the moon)
How can he literally get through to help people that want to commit suicide


Kanye has addressed the topic of suicide before in his music. Notably, on his 2012 song “Clique,” Ye raps about having suicidal urges following the death of his mother, Donda West, which is the central theme of Donda:

Went through, deep depression when my mama passed
Suicide, what kinda talk is that?

Similarly, Cudi has battled mental health and suicidal urges throughout his career. In March 2014, Cudi talked about wanting to provide guidance for young listeners with his music:

My mission statement since day one […] all I wanted to do was help kids not feel alone, and stop committing suicide.

line: Sippin’ on that Henn’
vault_lines: Sippin' on that Henn'
meaning:
“Henn'” is referring to Hennessy, a popular high-end brand of cognac. Cognac is a style of brandy liquor produced in the Cognac region of France.

Hennessy is often referred to in rap songs. According to District Magazine, in their June 2021 piece “How Hennessy became rap’s favourite drink”,


There are many layers to the story of hip hop and Black cultural affection for cognac in the US. One story goes that Black soldiers serving in the army brought home a taste for cognac after being stationed in France and getting it in their rations. Perhaps this French spirit appealed more than the brasher whiskeys of the day which had Southern and Confederacy associations, as I read in a 2013 Slate article.  During the post war period of consumer expansion in America, Hennessy actively pursued this new market by placing ads in prominent Black magazines such as Jet and Ebony. They worked with Black actors in their ads depicting aspirational African American lifestyles that was not portrayed in most advertising at the time.

Hennessy became a familiar, trusted brand that laid the groundwork for the late pop cultural ubiquity. The company employed a Black Vice President, an Olympian athlete named Herb Douglas, at a time when senior African American appointments were rare. Sales to this day provide strong evidence of its enduring popularity with African American consumers.

line: Her body must be recycled ’cause this bitch ain’t got no waist (Woo)
vault_lines: Her body must be recycled 'cause this bitch ain't got no waist (Woo)
meaning:
This part of the lyric uses “recycle” in a playful and layered way. Recycling involves processing materials to make them reusable. Metaphorically, it suggests that the woman’s body is incredibly well-shaped, as if it has been perfectly refined or reshaped. Additionally, “recycle” hints at the possibility that she has undergone a lot of plastic surgery, since plastic is a commonly recycled material. This adds a humorous twist, implying her perfect figure could be the result of cosmetic enhancements.

This phrase serves as a double entendre. On one level, it continues the metaphor by describing the woman’s physical appearance. Saying someone “ain’t got no waist” means their waist is extremely small or cinched, emphasizing a very slim, hourglass figure. The exaggeration implies that her waist is so small it appears almost non-existent, highlighting her curves. On another level, it plays on the word “waist” sounding like “waste.” By stating she “ain’t got no waist,” it also implies she has no waste, tying back to the recycling metaphor and suggesting she’s efficiently refined with nothing going to waste.
